subsystems.name: Generative backbone model
subsystems.role: invents the 3D shape of a protein that could perform the wanted job — for example, gripping a specific patch on a target.
parts: conditional constraints such as a target binding site
hallucination or inpainting routines for scaffolds

subsystems.name: Sequence design model
subsystems.role: picks the amino acid string that will fold into that shape.

subsystems.name: Structure prediction and filters
subsystems.role: checks whether the designed sequence really folds as intended before any wet-lab work.
parts: predictors such as AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold3

subsystems.name: Training and compute
subsystems.role: the data and hardware that make the models work.

subsystems.name: Synthesis and expression
subsystems.role: turns a designed sequence into physical protein.
parts: E. coli, yeast or cell-free expression

subsystems.name: Characterisation and assay
subsystems.role: measures whether the protein made actually works.
parts: binding assays such as surface plasmon resonance

buildSteps.title: Write the functional specification
buildSteps.detail: Define what the protein must do: which target surface to bind, the desired affinity (often nanomolar or tighter), the working temperature and pH, and the size limit for manufacture.

buildSteps.title: Generate candidate backbones
buildSteps.detail: A diffusion model is given the target structure and the binding site, and produces many possible protein folds — typically 50–100 amino acids for a binder — that present the right shape to that surface.

buildSteps.title: Design sequences for each backbone
buildSteps.detail: A sequence-design model such as ProteinMPNN proposes several amino acid sequences per backbone, choosing residues that stabilise the fold and pack well at the binding interface.

buildSteps.title: Filter in silico
buildSteps.detail: Each sequence is re-folded by a structure predictor and compared with the intended design; candidates with poor confidence, bad packing, exposed sticky patches or unstable regions are discarded.

buildSteps.title: Synthesise the genes
buildSteps.detail: Hundreds of surviving designs are ordered as synthetic DNA, codon-optimised for the chosen expression host.

buildSteps.title: Express and purify
buildSteps.detail: The genes are put into E. coli, yeast or a cell-free system, grown at small scale, and the proteins purified by affinity tags followed by size-exclusion chromatography.

buildSteps.title: Measure
buildSteps.detail: Binding affinity and kinetics are measured, often first in pooled high-throughput display assays and then individually; successful designs are checked structurally by cryo-EM or crystallography and for melting temperature.

buildSteps.title: Iterate
buildSteps.detail: Experimental results — which designs bound, how tightly, how stably — go back into the next round of design, or feed directed-evolution or affinity-maturation libraries.

buildSteps.title: Develop the winner
buildSteps.detail: The best candidate is engineered for manufacturing yield, shelf life and low immune reactivity, then tested in cells and animals before any human trial.

prerequisites.why: the Protein Data Bank supplies the experimental structures the models learn from.
AlphaFold2 in 2020 first made it possible to tell whether a designed sequence folds as intended, and the AlphaFold database holds predicted structures for over 200 million proteins.

prerequisites.tech: Diffusion and other generative deep learning
prerequisites.why: the same mathematics that generates images can generate physically plausible protein backbones.

prerequisites.tech: Cheap gene synthesis and high-throughput expression
prerequisites.why: design is useless without the ability to make and test hundreds of variants quickly.

prerequisites.tech: Reliable design of catalysis, not just binding
prerequisites.why: designing an enzyme that catalyses a chosen reaction with good rate and specificity remains much harder than designing a binder.

prerequisites.tech: Predicting immunogenicity and developability in humans
prerequisites.why: a protein that works in a test tube can still be cleared quickly or provoke an immune response in a patient.

pathway.milestone: generative design tools in routine laboratory and industry use; designed protein nanoparticle vaccines in clinical trials and a designed cytokine mimetic in early human testing
pathway.unlocks: much faster discovery of binders, vaccines and research reagents without waiting for nature to supply them.

pathway.milestone: a de novo designed protein approved as a medicine
pathway.unlocks: proof that computational design can survive manufacturing, regulation and human biology, not just the assay plate.

pathway.milestone: designed enzymes used in industrial chemistry and designed sensors and switches inside cells
pathway.unlocks: cleaner chemical routes and programmable biology beyond medicine.

pathway.milestone: closed-loop autonomous labs that design, make and test proteins without human intervention, including multi-domain machines and new materials
pathway.unlocks: design cycles measured in days, widening the search far beyond what any single team could test.
